en: Homage to the Blessed One, the Noble Mahāsāhasrapramardanī.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha,

on the Vulture Peak Mountain, on its southern slope, in the Radiant Grove near the Jewel Tree, within the domain of the Buddhas, together with a great community of monks, numbering twelve hundred and fifty, such as the venerable Śāriputra.
And with the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
the Venerable Mahākāśyapa,
and the Venerable Gayākāśyapa.
And with the Venerable Nadīkāśyapa,
the Venerable Urubilvākāśyapa,
and the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
And with the venerable Mahākātyāyana,
and with the venerable Vakula,
and with the venerable Vāṣpa.
And with the Venerable Koṣṭhila,
the Venerable Vāgīśa,
and the Venerable Aśvajit.
And with the Venerable Subhūti,
and the Venerable Suvāhu,
and the Venerable Aniruddha.
And with the Venerable Revata,
the Venerable Nandika, and the Venerable Ānanda.
At that time, with twelve hundred and fifty monks as his principal followers, the Blessed One, together with the community of monks,
was honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, adored, and supplicated by King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha with robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
At that time, in the great city of Vaiśālī, there was a great earthquake and a mass of clouds appeared.
A great, untimely wind and thunderbolt arose, a massive cloud gathered, the sky roared and rumbled, and flashes of lightning issued forth.
The ten directions became turbulent, and a blinding darkness appeared.
The constellations do not speak;
the moon and sun do not shine, do not heat, do not radiate, and do not become luminous.

Then the Blessed One, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, saw those terrors that had appeared in the great city of Vaiśālī. He saw how some of the Licchavis of Vaiśālī were possessed and afflicted by impure spirits;
and he saw [the same among] some of the village youths, as well as the accountants, chief ministers, ministers, courtiers, female slaves, male slaves, laborers, messengers, and attendants.

Overwhelmed on all sides by these spirits, the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen in the district of Vaiśālī became afraid, terrified, and agitated; with the hair on their bodies standing on end, they cried out with upturned faces and paid homage to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
And those brahmins and householders who have not taken refuge in the Buddha’s teaching—even among them, some brahmins and householders pay homage to Brahmā;
others pay homage to Śakra, some to the World-Protectors (Lokapālas);

and others again [pay homage] to Maheśvara, Māṇibhadra, Pūrṇabhadra, Hārītī, the moon, the sun, the planets, the constellations, mountains, groves, medicinal herbs, trees, rivers, springs, lakes, ponds, wells, tanks, and sacred shrines (caityasthāna).
They even pay homage, thinking:
"How might it be that we ourselves are liberated from such a calamity and from this place of fear?"
Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of supernatural power that, by means of that manifested supernatural power,
he made himself heard throughout the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system with his voice, and having inspired faith in the world of gods, humans, and asuras,
he caused them to assemble.
Then Brahmā Sahāpati, the gods of the Brahma-realm, Śakra the lord of the gods and the Trāyastriṃśa gods,

the four Great Kings and the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm, the twenty-eight great yakṣa generals, the thirty-two great yakṣa leaders, and Hārītī with her sons and her retinue— possessing surpassing beauty— [appeared] when the night had passed.
During the night, at the break of dawn, having illuminated Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa with their own majestic splendor and sublime radiance,
they approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, they stood to one side and, with one voice, one tone, and in unison, praised the Blessed One with verses.
Resplendent like glowing gold, radiant as the full moon,
the form of the hero appeared in sight like the glorious Vaiśravaṇa, a treasury of jewels.
With the prowess of a lion, an elephant, and a rutting lordly elephant,
he was like a mountain of gold or a necklace of Jambūnada gold.
Or like the moon in a cloudless sky, preceded by the stars.
In the midst of the community of disciples, he was fully adorned with the [major] marks.
Indeed, this world together with its gods has come for refuge to the Sage;
the time for protection has arrived for the sake of the welfare of human beings.
The *Sāhasrapramardanī* Sūtra has been proclaimed by all the Buddhas;
it is the supreme boundary-binding that extends as far as the Cakravāḍa mountains.
Homage to you, O hero among men; homage to you, the supreme among men.
With palms joined in reverence, we pay homage to the Great Sage, the King of Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having consented by remaining silent for a moment, addressed the four great kings.
"Great Kings, it would not be fitting for you that you should think our assembly ought to be harassed by your assembly.
Why is that?
Because it is here in the human world that there is the arising of a Buddha, the well-expounded Dharma, and the well-practiced Saṅgha."
Having planted this seed in this [field], the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, arise in the world;

and likewise the Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and Śrāvakas. Having planted roots of merit in this, these beings become kings in one or another of the thirty-two classes of gods, or they become universal monarchs (cakravartins) possessing the fourfold army and ruling over the four continents.
They shall rule the great circle of the earth, bounded by the ocean, according to the Dharma.

They will have a thousand sons who are heroic, brave, endowed with excellent physical forms, possessing the strength and speed of great athletes, crushers of enemy armies, and possessed of the seven jewels.
Therefore, while you dwell in a state of little concern, such beings as these will not arise in this world.

Then the Great King Vaiśravaṇa, rising from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, paid homage to the Blessed One and addressed him as follows.

"Venerable Blessed One, we have magnificent residences for householders—cities, gardens, celestial palaces, gabled halls, upper chambers, turrets, gateways, and windows—adorned with beautiful and pleasing various multicolored silk streamers, bells, chowries, and nets of pearls; they are perfumed by incense burners and strewn with flowers, wherein we dwell surrounded by hundreds of thousands of women, fully endowed and possessed of the five complete qualities of sensual pleasure."
"Venerable Blessed One, while we were dwelling thus, heedless and living in negligence, our retinue searched for food and drink from all ten directions.

Fleeing in terror, they seized the vital energy (*ojas*) of men, women, boys, and girls; they also robbed, harassed, obstructed, killed, and deprived of life even those beings born as animals, those conceived in the wombs of animals, and those belonging to the animal realm."

"Venerable One, in the presence of the Blessed One, we shall display the physical characteristics of our respective assemblies before the fourfold assembly. Whichever assembly has a particular affinity for a certain [deity],
then a magnificent caitya and image of that great king must be constructed."
And with the hand of that afflicted person, various fragrant incenses should be burned in the name of that great king.
Having performed the *dhāraṇī* by scattering flowers and having lit lamps, worship should be offered there at the shrine (*caitya*).
"Venerable Blessed One, such are the physical characteristics of one from my assembly who has been seized by a *yakṣa*-graha."
He laughs and trembles repeatedly, prattles on and becomes agitated;
sleep overcomes him, or a piercing pain arises.
He constantly gazes upward and pursues the stars;
at night he experiences great joy, and he is always trembling and gasping.
In this regard, O Lord of the World, there are mantra-words; listen to me.
It may be as follows:
Siddhe / Susiddhe / Satve Are / Araṇe.
Bale! Mahābale! Jambhe! Stambhe! Jaṭile!
In digging,
in sacrificing,
in eating.
Kharaṭṭe / kharaṅge / haripiṅgale timiṅgile svāhā!
May my mantra-words be effective; may there be well-being for me and for all sentient beings, by the name, power, sovereignty, and lordship of the Great King Vaiśravaṇa, svāhā!

Then the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having risen from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, paid homage to the Blessed One and addressed him as follows:
"Venerable Blessed One, such are the physical characteristics of one possessed by a *gandharva-graha* from among our assembly:
he dances and sings, takes pleasure in ornaments,
is free from greed and speaks the truth, yet laughs and becomes angry again."
His eyes become bloodshot with thirst, and fever constantly overcomes him;
his eyes do not open, and he lies sleeping with his face turned away.
In this regard, there are mantra-words; O Lord of the World, listen to me.
It may be as follows:
*akhe*, *nakhe*, *vinakhe*, *bandhe*.
O Varāṇī!
O Capalā!
O Vakhe!
In the month of Vākhaṇa,
Vākhiṇa, or Akhina.
In the nails, in the calves, and in the private parts.
To Bhagandara, to Vaśa, to Vaśavartinī, svāhā!
May all sentient beings be liberated from all seizing spirits by the name, power, sovereignty, and lordship of the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra; svāhā!

Then the Great King Virūḍhaka rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, paid homage to the Blessed One and addressed him thus:
"Venerable Blessed One, such are the physical characteristics of one seized by a *kumbhāṇḍa* spirit from our assembly:
they experience intense thirst and look about with a bewildered gaze;
their face appears blood-red and they sleep curled up upon the ground."
They are ill-favored in complexion, with emaciated limbs, long hair and nails, foul-smelling, and filthy; moreover, they speak with utter confusion.
In this regard, O Lord of the World, there are mantra-words; listen to me.
It may be as follows:
*khakhakhame*, *khalane*.
In the threshing floor; in the hair of the threshing floor;
in the drawing of the donkey.
Kharakhe / Khaṭine / Kharali.
Karakhi, kaśane, karaṭe.
O Beloved, at the right time! O Dispeller!
O Ordainer!
Obedient one!
O you who lie down!
O you who are equanimous!
To Śamī, to Śaminī, svāhā!
May all seizing spirits, all fears, and all calamities of myself and of all sentient beings be pacified by the name, power, sovereignty, and lordship of the Great King Virūḍhaka; svāhā!

Then the great king Virūpākṣa rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and, extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, paid homage to the Blessed One.
He said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Blessed One, such are the physical characteristics of one from our assembly who has been seized by a *nāga* or a *suparṇin*:
he hiccups, gasps for breath, and his body becomes cold."
He perspires with frothy saliva and falls asleep again and again.
He becomes handsome and brave, then trembles and runs;
again he shows his nails, enters the earth, and weeps.
In this regard, there are mantra-words; O Lord of the World, listen to me.
It may be as follows:
*kragame*, *krakamaṇi*, *krakase*.
Krakaśase! Kruśume! Krukeke!
Krukhume krume / agale / nagale /
Samaṅgale / Kuhume / Hume /
In the *āluke*,
in the *kalalaka*, in the *kalala*.
Ire mire / dhire dhire agaruvati svāhā //
May there be well-being for me and for all sentient beings, through the name, power, sovereignty, and lordship of the Great King Virūpākṣa; svāhā!
Then, right there before the entire assembly, the Blessed One let out a lion’s roar:
"Endowed with the ten powers and confident in the four grounds of self-confidence, I let out the noble, bull-like, true lion’s roar in the assembly;
I turn the Wheel of Brahmā."
Māra, along with his army, strength, and vehicles, has been conquered by me alone;
for the protection of all sentient beings, you all should listen to my vidyā.
It may be thus:
O Unattached One! O You who possess the sword! O Powerful One!
O you whose roar is power!
O hero! O you who possess heroism!
O you who move with the adamantine gait!
O Vajradhara! O Stambha! O Jambha! O Dṛḍhasāra!
O Virajā!
O Vighase!
O Varāgraprāptā!
In the direction free from strife and endowed with Dharma, which is proclaimed far and wide—svāhā!
May there be well-being for me and for all sentient beings, by the name, power, sovereignty, and lordship of the Tathāgata; svāhā!
Having heard the words of the Buddha, the world-protectors stood in the four directions, trembling, terrified, and deeply agitated, with their palms joined in reverence.
The remaining hosts of spirits, terrified, scattered, and dispersed,
fled in the ten directions, uttering a great cry.
Having understood that, the Great King proclaimed the triple protection:
"O, this is the knowledge, the great knowledge, the crusher of the great trichiliocosm!"
Upon hearing the Buddha’s speech, living beings tremble,
just as a blazing fire is fanned by the winds.
This knowledge, equal to the edge of a razor, has been revealed by Gautama;
for whoever would not hold this well-spoken word of the Sage in high esteem.
Due to a Brahmin’s curse, he shall have no eldest son;
however, having kindled a fire and taken black mustard seeds, [he should proceed].
These, combined with the scum of clarified butter, should be cast into the fire;
having sprinkled water from the Varuṇa-vessel below, above, and in the four directions.
If, having heard the Buddha’s speech, they do not release [me] quickly,
may they all become ablaze like ghee and mustard seeds in a fire.
Threatened by the punishment of the yakṣas, they will obtain safety;
however, on their right sides, there will arise a great swelling.
Afflicted by the yakṣa-disease, they will become disfigured and will never again go to the royal capital, Aḍakavatī.
The hosts of spirits will not see the residence of the illustrious Kubera,
nor will they obtain a seat in the assembly.
Deprived of food and drink, they are born in the realm of the yakṣas;
whichever yakṣa does not comply with this *Mahāsāhasrapramardanī Sūtra* [shall suffer such a fate].
The wrathful Vajradhara will split his head open;
here, with a blade as sharp as a harsh razor, he shall cut out his tongue.
With a sharp weapon he shall cut off his ears and nose;
with a razor-edged wheel he shall cause his head to fall.
One should also press upon his heart with an iron hammer and wedge;
then, from his mouth, pus and warm blood shall flow forth.
Bound by the noose of ignorance and the staff, those who always wander in saṃsāra will continue to revolve within that very cycle of existence, in the mandala of saṃsāra.
(Msp 8) Possessed of splendor, the great kings assembled from the four directions;
armored with the armor of the Dharma, they sat upon auspicious thrones.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra is in the east, Virūḍhaka in the south,
Virūpākṣa in the west, and Kubera in the northern direction.
While the kings had assembled, blazing with splendor and majesty,
the Teacher, the Omniscient One, indeed arose in the midst of the sky.
Having sat here upon the vajra-throne in this celestial palace fashioned by Brahmā,
the Great Brahmā then stands with palms joined in reverence and pays homage.
The glorious mountain of gold, resembling molten gold,
was in full bloom like a lotus flower, or like a king of *śāla* trees covered in blossoms.
Like the full moon or the sun surrounded by the constellations,
the Sage is encompassed by a body of golden hue and adorned with the primary marks.
Having praised the Illuminator of the World, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the World,
then spoke to the world-protectors in the presence of the Lord of the World.
Neither the assembly nor the instruction of the World-Protectors has been attained;
for from here indeed are born the Buddhas, as well as the Pratyekabuddhas.
From this [source] also arise the śrāvakas, and the gods likewise emerge;
from this are born the brahmins who have mastered the Vedas along with their six auxiliary branches.
And the highly fortunate sages, as well as these ascetics and brahmins here,
will procreate human offspring for you who are free from anxiety.
Having heard the words of Brahmā, the world-protectors spoke these words:
"So it is, O Great Brahmā; so it is, O Great Sage."
Having caused Mount Sumeru to tremble and having mastered the dhāraṇīs, we shall purify this ocean on all sides.
We shall bind the moon, the sun, and likewise the wind with a noose, as well as all the constellations, with a firm and tightly applied cord.
We shall always regard as non-existent those regions and their parts who will be corrupt and not intent on the welfare of the world.
For this world, including the gods, censures one for the sake of elemental beings;
indeed, elemental beings bring about ruin and harm the human population.
In this regard, those who hold the mantras may indeed display their prowess;
yet they overstep [the bounds] if they transgress against the *vidyā*, the mantras, or even the medicinal herbs.
Having threatened the assemblies on all sides with our staffs, we shall bring those who have transgressed against knowledge before the Lord of the World.
We shall pronounce punishment upon them by means of this Sūtra fashioned by Brahmā,
which, when recited, threatens the entire circle of living beings.
Having prostrated at the feet of the Buddha and looked at one another,
[they offered] gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, and crystal.
He prepared four well-constructed golden chariots, adorned with the seven precious gems, featuring wheels made of emerald and possessing a thousand spokes.
Having ascended there— those who were engaged in various crafts and possessed the power of moving through the air— the kings departed for the realm of the spirits.
Having covered the earth with flowers and even with golden powders,
and having tied staffs as well as cords of thread around their necks;
Having dispatched all the yakṣa generals to the four directions, [command]:
"Bring forth all beings, however many there are, who have come from our direction!"
For this supreme sūtra, the *Sāhasrapramardanī*,
has arisen from the Brahma-world and is cherished by all the worlds.
Having heard the words of Kubera, the yakṣa general, accompanied by a body of a thousand great beings, went forth and crushed the yakṣas and rākṣasas.
O Sage, as they advance in the four directions, the Guhyakas, the twenty-eight Bhūtas, and the Gandharva-born Grahas raise a great clamor.
In this eastern direction, may the hosts of spirits listen to me:
all of you are bound by the noose of the Sūtra and oppressed by the fivefold fetters.
And there are twenty-eight spirits, O Sage, born of the Kumbhāṇḍas;
let the hosts of beings in this southern quarter listen to me.
All of them are bound by the snare of the sutra and oppressed by the five fetters;
and the twenty-eight classes of spirits, O Sage, become Naga-grahas.
In this western quarter, may the hosts of spirits listen to me!
O Sage, all those twenty-eight classes of spirits and yakṣa-seizers are bound by the snare of the sutra and oppressed by the fivefold bonds.
And let the hosts of beings in the northern quarter also listen to me.
All of them were bound by the noose of the Sūtra and oppressed by the fivefold bonds;
they were Sañjaya, the eldest son of Kubera, who is carried by men.
At his very feet, sixty million yakṣas were drawn in by the noose of the mantra-cord, tormented by the fivefold bonds.
His second son was the renowned Janaka;
at his very feet were sixty million yakṣas.
Drawn in by the noose of the thread and oppressed by the five bonds,
he is the third son of that very one, and he is that great graha by name.
At his very feet, sixty million yakṣas were drawn in by the noose of the mantra-cord, tormented by the fivefold bond.
His fourth son was Kalaśodara by name;
at his very feet were sixty million yakṣas.
Drawn in by the noose of the thread and oppressed by the fivefold bonds are Maheśvara,
Mahādeva, the four-armed one of great strength.
At his very feet, sixty million yakṣas were drawn in by the noose of the mantra-thread, tormented by the fivefold bond.
Having come to the mountain Bhūtamardana, all beings proclaimed this Vidyā, which is the sovereign knowledge that bestows peace upon all.
For this harsh punishment for men has been proclaimed by all the Buddhas;
therefore, let us all go with reverence to Gautama for refuge.
"Follow me without guile, and do not fear anything.
Then, in just a moment, the hosts of spirits assembled.
Those who dwell upon the mountains, in precipices, in oceans, and in lakes; in rivers, springs, and pools, and in whirlpools.
Those who dwell in gardens, celestial palaces, groves, and forests; in sacred shrines, villages, and at the roots of trees.
Those who were stationed at the entrances of the city, in the towns and districts,
at the royal palaces, at the gates, and in the celestial mansions;
In pavilions, in cremation grounds, and likewise in temples; at boundaries, in customs houses, in empty dwellings, and in desolate wildernesses.
The yakṣas who are above and below, and those in the four cardinal directions and the intermediate directions—
thousands of millions of yakṣas drawn by the noose of knowledge.
Having played the mṛdaṅga drums, some played the gargara drums;
those of great strength also played the vīṇā, paṇava, and flutes.
And having performed various musical performances, as well as song and dance,
Indra, Soma, Varuṇa, Bharadvāja, and Prajāpati [were present].
Mātali, Lohitākṣa, Himavant, Supūrṇaka, Candana, Kāmaśreṣṭhin, Maṇikaṇṭha, and Nikaṇṭhaka.
The preceptor of creatures, the lord of ascetics, Mātali the charioteer of the gods,
the Gandharva Citrasena, and Nararāja Jinarṣabha.
Likewise, there were Tumburu named Pañcaśikha, Sūryavarcas,
Śaila, Asiputra, Viśvāmitra, and Yaśodhara.
Āḍavaka, Sumanas, Śūcīkarṇa, Darīmukha,
Pañcālagaṇḍa, and Sumukha, together with their armies, forces, and vehicles.
The gods, nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, yakṣas, and rākṣasas;
the tertian fevers, madnesses, and likewise the quartan fevers.
And those wicked yakṣas and rākṣasas who harass the world,
having been summoned from the four directions, are tormented by the fivefold bonds.
Standing before him with palms joined in reverence, they then addressed the Lord of the World:
"Homage to you, O hero among men; homage to you, O supreme among men!"
With palms joined in reverence, we pay homage; O Dharmarāja, let there be salutation to you!
Terrifying spirits and yakṣas run ahead of them.
Four-armed and most terrible, with many feet or a single foot;
four-footed and two-footed, with feet turned upward or faces turned downward.
Some have many bodies with a single head, while others have a single body with four heads;
some have many eyes and massive bodies, while others have a single eye and twelve bellies.
The Rākṣasas had the heads of donkeys, camels, and elephants; their hands were raised upward while their heads hung down;
they had weapons for teeth, weapons for arms, and weapons for feet.
They have copper-colored hair, copper-colored hands, copper-colored eyes, and copper-colored palms;
their feet are like copper hammers, their noses are copper, and their mouths are iron.
With hands and feet ablaze, they exist in human form;
some are one-eyed, others are hunchbacked, while the Garuḍas and the Vijṛmbhakas have deformed eyes.
They have the forms of sea-monsters and beasts of prey, being deformed with their faces turned upward;
they have hanging lips, crooked teeth, and are malevolent with frowning faces.
They had large bellies, ears like jars, long ears, or no ears at all;
they had long ears, long arms, and hands with long fingertips.
With withered bodies, tall statures, and long hair, though well-adorned;
burdened by their feet, with thin necks, foul-smelling, and possessing hands as large as bellies.
Some had the appearance of crocodiles, while others resembled pestles, mallets, or the bellies [of such tools];
they had eyes turned upward, large ears, hair standing erect, and were deep red in color.
With thick heads, bow-shaped necks, hunchbacks, pot-bellies, and emaciated bodies,
they indeed rained down showers of fire after surveying the summit of Mount Meru.
The peaks and summits of trees, mountains, and rocks possess a uniform radiance;
the kumbhāṇḍas have voices like conchs, kettledrums, clay drums, and celestial drums.
Those with great throats and harsh voices let out a terrifying roar;
they were black, blue, yellow, green, and tawny-brown.
The Guhyakas stand before the abode of all the wicked;
they devour the human world, as well as men, women, and others.
Others had their flesh, blood, fat, and marrow hacked away;
they were covered with needles, hair, and body-hair, and smeared with red blood.
Devouring and indeed seizing upon corpses, they run about—
those with sharp teeth and blood-stained hands, their lips smeared with gore.
With their limbs half-devoured and their hands filled [with flesh],
they were devouring the kidneys, hearts, collarbones, and thighs.
Terrible with their hands and feet, they carry off the strength of living beings;
with bodies composed of heaps of bones, they terrify many people.
Taking a human skin filled with blood and smeared with fierce poison, they fling it in the ten directions.
Entering into cities, they scatter from house to house;
they agitate the wind, bile, and phlegm in the four directions.
Thus, there arise great fears of oppression by kings;
even all those who have assembled together are dragged away by the noose of the vidyā-mantra.
Homage to you, O hero among men; homage be to you, O supreme among men!
With palms joined in reverence, we pay homage to you, O King of Dharma; homage be to you!
Terrible yakṣas who steal vitality and subsist on human flesh and blood roam through cities, villages, kingdoms, and royal palaces.
They have massive bodies, are most terrifying, possess great strength, and are supreme lords;
they have ten necks, a thousand eyes, enormous appetites, and vast mouths.
With a great retinue, they were most terrifying, holding weapons in their hands;
four-armed, they grasped snake-skins and carried torches in their hands.
With staffs in hand, weapons in hand, bearing spears and thunderbolts in their palms,
they cause all directions to tremble with great terror, brandishing their most dreadful arms.
All the Guhyakas, though dwelling in the abode of the wicked, become gracious;
they devour men, women, and others in the world of humans.
With limbs glowing from hot flesh and blood, they can assume any form at will;
they take the shapes of lions, tigers, buffaloes, cows, donkeys, camels, and elephants.
With the forms of bears, leopards, wolves, antelopes, jackals, rams, and cats; resembling mice and monkeys; and with rhinoceroses, boars, and mongooses.
And with others in the forms of fish and tortoises, crows and cuckoos,
as well as owls, vultures, cranes, and so forth, and likewise timis and timiṅgilas.
Some yakṣas behold human beings in the forms of peacocks, swans, pigeons, and cranes; others do so in the form of cocks.
In the guise of garuḍas, they terrify many people;
some have human heads and bodies as fierce as wild asses,
while others with distorted intentions are seen rushing about in various ways.
Naked, devoted solely to sensual desires, and draped with garlands of entrails.
They strike with tridents and inflict suffering upon living beings;
they let out a terrible gasp and torment these creatures.
As many as there are successions of living beings, they are seen in various forms:
some are carrying mountains, while others bear swords and wheels.
Numbering hundreds of thousands, the rākṣasas were threatened with pestles and clubs; their eyes were gouged out, they were turned away in defeat, and their teeth were shattered.
With their noses severed, their ears severed, their tongues severed, and their faces wrinkled;
with their hands and feet cut off, and their heads severed—such were the rākṣasas.
For those wicked ones indeed watch for a lapse and destroy the vital energy;
the seizure within the bodies of humans is seen to be extremely subtle.
They all gathered together within the pores of his hair, at his vital points, and likewise at the openings of his wounds, having been drawn forth by the noose of his vidyā-mantra.
Homage to you, O hero among men; homage to you, O supreme among men.
With palms joined in reverence, we pay homage; O King of Dharma, let there be homage to you!
And on Sumeru, the king of mountains, and likewise on Cakravāḍa,

On Mount Pāṇḍava and on Citrakūṭa— on these two mountains—

The deities who were there below, as well as the sages who were likewise superior,
became agitated, their minds terrified for their own lives.
Thousands of millions of gods and hundreds of millions of gods,
along with highly fortunate celestial maidens, indeed joined their palms in reverent salutation.
Vemacitrin, Rāhula, and Prahlāda have assembled,
accompanied by thousands of crores of servants and even hundreds of crores of servants.
Their daughters, endowed with supernatural powers, joined their ten fingers in salutation;
so too did Sāgara, Supratiṣṭha, and the wise Nāga king Manasvin.
Nagendra and Anavatapta, both Nanda and Upanandaka,

The Suparṇīs, the kings of birds, who agitate the ocean along with thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of nāgas.
Their highly fortunate daughters, having indeed joined their palms in reverence,
[beheld] both the sun and the moon surrounded by the host of constellations.
Suvarṇavarṇa was among the Puṣpas, Rabheyaka among the Magadhas, Kāpila among the Bharukacchas, and Prapuṇḍaka among the Kośalas.

Vibhīṣaṇa among the Pañcālas, and Lohitākṣa among the Aśvakas.
Piṅgala was among the Avantis, Kapilākṣa in Vaidiśa, Kumbhodara among the Matsyas, and Dīrghila among the Sūras.
Pramardana is in Gāndhāra, and Sūryamitra is among the Kambus;
these are said to be the fourteen yakṣas in the great provinces.
Vajrapāṇi, the great yakṣa, Dharmapāla, Prapuṇḍara,
Kapila, Sudarśana, Viṣṇu, Piṇḍāra, and Karaśodara.
Kumbhīra, Sātyaki, and Pāñcika, the bull among Jinas;

Pramardana, Śūrasena, Mahānagna, and Mahābala; Yama, Yamadūta, and Māra together with his army.
That yakṣa named Hari is accompanied by a retinue of ten million yakṣas;
likewise are Hārītī with her army and the yakṣiṇī Giridāri.
She is of terrifying form and great splendor, renowned by the name Hārītī;
she is fierce and a slayer of the fierce, surrounded by five hundred sons.
Ākoṭā, Karkaṭī, Kālī, Padumā, Padumāvatī, Puṣpadantī, Viśālā, and the Rākṣasī Kharakarṇā.
Candana, Viṣṇula, Haripiṅgalapiṅgala,
Kuñjara, Nāgadanta, Girimitra, and Agradaṃṣṭraka.
The rākṣasīs Bhadradantā and Brahmilā, as well as Viṣṇulā;
the yakṣa Hālāhala and the rākṣasa Vituṇḍaka.
Then, seizing cows, buffaloes, deer, and humans upon their spears,
they ran in every direction, devouring them while still alive.
Trembling, they wither the *dhāraṇīs* and the lords of the forest;
they cause the mountain peaks to crumble and crush these living beings.
Drawing one another together by means of spells, they assembled; for when they had thus gathered before the Lord of the World, they rejoiced in mutual delight.
Then King Vaiśravaṇa spoke to the Lord of the World:
"In my northern region, there is a well-constructed royal capital."
Because Manoramā-Aḍakavatī was thought of by all the gods, I am the Lord of Aḍakā; the royal capital is indeed called Aḍakā.
The ramparts were raised high, adorned with the seven precious gems,
and embellished at every two yojanas with golden *kṣaumaka* ornaments.
And in each of the four directions surrounding the *kṣomaka*,
there stand yakṣas who are wielders of the vajra, holding weapons in their hands and clad in fine armor.
At that very capital city, four gates were constructed:
one gate was made of gold, and the second was fashioned of silver.
The third gate is made of crystal, and the fourth is adorned with jewels;
within the city, however, there is a park with forests in full bloom.
The celestial palaces are indeed variegated and composed of the seven precious gems;
there are trees made of various jewels, resounding with the songs of diverse birds.
Covered with various flowers, anointed with various fragrant unguents,
and adorned with the playful movements of birds as well as songs and instrumental music.
I experience supreme glory among all beings in that mandala;
my attendants there are endowed with the excellence of all forms.
Those who practice the Dharma and desire the Dharma do not harm living beings;
however, other, more cruel creatures are deprived of food and drink.
Practicing unrighteousness and desiring what is unrighteous, they cause harm to living beings;
seeking something sublime, they gaze in the four directions.
Those thousands of millions of hosts of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and bhūtas who reside at the city gates, as well as in the gardens and forests—
I shall bring them all here, drawn in by the noose of my sutra,
to this place covered with groves of sandalwood trees and filled with cool lotus ponds.
In the center of that royal capital was the residence of the King of Dharma;
for a distance of one yojana all around, gabled chambers were constructed,
one of which was made of gold and the second of silver.
The third is of vaidūrya, while the fourth is pure crystal.
The fifth is made of red pearl, the sixth of emerald (*aśmagarbha*),
the seventh of beryl (*musāra*), and the eighth consists of the seven precious gems.
Hundreds of thousands of women gathered at each [place],
adorned with various excellent ornaments and various wonderful garments.
Trained in various songs, instrumental music, and the arts,
they were uplifted by such delight, their minds filled with joy.
There, excessively intoxicated by the drinking of honey-wine and by sensual pleasures,
my assembly fled away and terrified the ten directions.
Both women and men, as well as boys and girls—
even those still in the womb and even those born as animals— perish.
The stars, the moon, the sun, and the planets become cruel and cause affliction;
they likewise afflict the grain, the seed, the fruit, the flower, the medicinal herb, and food and drink.
They carry away human prosperity and cause it to rise and fall;
whatever misdeeds there are in the world, such as enmities, quarrels, and conflicts—[they bring these about].
That which is burnt, lost, killed, or broken—all that is known to be born of the elements;
they cover themselves, uncover themselves, turn over, and remain still.
They terrify sentient beings, they stare at them, and they harbor hatred;
they show them evil dreams and afflict them while they sleep.
Standing at the gates, they snap their fingers, shouting and devouring;
appearing in the forms of friends and kinsmen, they are seen and they speak.
Assuming forms at will, they appear in the form of various maidens;
they appear in the form of the moon, and in the form of the sun and the stars.
Afflicting the wind, they appear in the form of wind-flames and thunderbolts;
resembling a mass of meteors, they are as terrifying as the howl of jackals.
And they are seen striding about among trees, shrines, and dwellings,
appearing in the form of youths, blazing with light and sounding like carts.
These seizing spirits always display various forms upon the dwellings and the paths;
they release them at the doors of houses and cities.
Having seized the life-force and the body, they lead them away onto evil paths.
And various forms, and various sounds.
They display various ailments and indeed diseases situated within the body;
they also display the contrary characteristics in all illnesses.
Whatever natures exist in the world, they display them all otherwise;
even though they have all come together, they are drawn in by the noose of knowledge.

Then the Blessed One said this:

"The Buddha-Blessed Ones do not appear in the world for the sake of a single king; nor do they appear in the world for the sake of a single city, market town, district, village, or family, up to and including for the sake of a single sentient being."

Rather, for the sake of the world with its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās, and for the sake of this generation of recluses and brahmins, including gods, humans, and asuras, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, arise in the world.

Just as there might be a physician, a healer, a supreme teacher, skilled in medical knowledge and trained in the arts of healing, they do not arise in the world for the sake of a single king or for the sake of a single being.
In the same way, the Buddha Bhagavāns arise in the world.
For what reason? Because in whichever direction the Buddha Bhagavāns dwell, [in that direction they appear].
He does not consider that humans or non-humans there should be harmed:
"For five days I shall proceed toward the great city of Vaiśālī;
thus, for the sake of the great multitude in the great city of Vaiśālī, I shall have performed the work of a Buddha."
Then, indeed, in the forenoon, the Blessed One, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, descended from Vulture Peak Mountain together with twelve hundred and fifty monks.
Then Brahmā Sahāpati, taking five hundred divine parasols, offered them to the Blessed One on his right side;
having offered them, he stood there fanning the Blessed One.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, also took up about five hundred parasols and presented them to the Blessed One from the left side;
having presented them, he stood there fanning the Blessed One.
Each of the four great kings also took five hundred divine parasols and presented them to the Blessed One from behind; having presented them, they stood fanning the Blessed One himself.

The divine son Maheśvara, the twenty-eight great yakṣa generals, the thirty-two great yakṣa nāgas, and Hārītī together with her sons and her retinue, each presented a divine parasol to the śrāvakas and stood there victorious.

Having thus attained the highest degree of fame, gain, and honor, the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, descended from Vulture Peak Mountain and proceeded toward the great city of Vaiśālī.

Then the Licchavis of Vaiśālī saw the Blessed One approaching from afar— gracious and inspiring, with senses calmed and mind tranquil, with senses subdued and mind tamed, having attained the supreme and most excellent self-mastery and serenity.

With his senses conquered like a well-tamed elephant, as clear and serene as a limpid lake, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and variegated by the eighty secondary characteristics—
like a king of *śāla* trees in full bloom, or like the sun in the sky releasing its web of rays during the day— such was the body of the Tathāgata.
And at night, during the pitch-black darkness, standing upon a mountain peak,
he kindled a great mass of fire,
like a vast mountain of refined gold.
In just this way, the Blessed One speaks, shines, and radiates; as soon as they saw him, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī set their minds at peace in the presence of the Blessed One.
With hearts full of serene faith, they cleared and swept the path by which the Blessed One was entering the great city of Vaiśālī,
and they made it most excellent, strewn with flowers.
Having raised up various silk streamers, bells, parasols, banners, and flags, and having perfumed the area with various scents and incense, they approached the Blessed One;
having approached, they prostrated their heads at the feet of the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, having raised up those Licchavis by stroking their heads with his hand— whose palm was marked with the beautiful thousand-spoked wheel, which was as tender as the interior of a lotus bud, accumulated through the marks of former good deeds, possessing a radiance exceeding the rays of the young sun, and stainless with hundreds of thousands of spreading beams— he exhorted them.
"Do not fear, do not fear! Noble ones, come here; I have arrived out of compassion for you alone. I have awakened to unsurpassed knowledge for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings."

Then the Blessed One, having entered the great city of Vaiśālī, stood upon the threshold of the city gate during the middle watch of the night. Looking toward the four directions and extending his gold-colored arm, he adjusted his upper robe and said:

"Whoever, in the future time, in the final age, shall worship even a relic of the Tathāgata the size of a mustard seed, and [whoever shall uphold] this *Mahāsāhasrapramardanī*, the Queen of Spells, the Dharma-discourse that liberates from all seizing spirits..."
The monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen shall take up, uphold, recite, teach, and master the Buddha-seal of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, who are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

For them, everywhere— fear, calamity, misfortune, distress, enmity, strife, quarrel, imprisonment, conflict, and dispute, and even at the very least, slanderous, evil, unwholesome, and painful conditions— shall not prevail.
And they shall be invincible against all who would cause them harm.

For those who, with minds full of serene faith and firm resolve, have approached the teaching of Gautama.

This is the sublime and excellent Jewel of the Saṅgha; by this truth, may there be well-being here!

This is the sublime and excellent Jewel of the Saṃgha; by this truth, may there be well-being here!

May all sentient beings here—both those that move and those that are stationary—be happy.

By that very truth by which the Conqueror has overcome his enemies—that speaker of truth has no enemy.
By that very truth, may there be well-being here; may all be liberated today from great fears, svāhā!

O Mahābrahman, this is that queen of vidyās named Mahāsāhasrapramardanī, the sūtra that liberates from all seizing spirits; it is the seal of the Buddhas and the footprint of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā.
The words of the Dharma; the words of the Saṅgha; the words of Brahmā.
The station of Indra; the station of the World-Protectors;
the station of Īśvara.
The state of a great seer; the state of one who seeks the ultimate; the state of the future.
The word for the eye,
the word for the cause,
the word for the location.
These are the words of exposition;
they are the words of perfect awakening,
touched by both the perfectly awakened Buddhas and the Pratyekabuddhas.
It is empowered by the śrāvakas,
praised by the Brahmās,
and honored by Indra.
She is saluted by the world-protectors,
worshipped by Īśvara,
and praised by all the gods.
Rejoiced in by the practitioners of yoga,
adorned by the seers,
and praised by the Brahmās.
It was contemplated by the deities,
praised by those who have completed their studies,
and [honored] by the world of the four castes.
It is the domain of all Buddhas,
the pleasure grove of Pratyekabuddhas,
and the departure of Śrāvakas.
It is the support for practitioners of yoga,
the source of the factors conducive to awakening,
and the stream that carries away the afflictions.
It is the uprooting of the thorns of latent tendencies,
the revealing of the gates to liberation,
and the shattering of the views of a self-existent body.
It is the felling of the mountain of pride,
the opening of the noble path,
and the closing of the gates to liberation.
It is the drying up of the ocean of saṃsāra; the removal of the mountains of bones of all those fallen into saṃsāra;
and the severing of Māra’s snare.
It terrifies the assembly of Māra;
it swallows up the hook of Māra;
it strikes terror into the battle of the afflictions.
It is that which leads into the city of Nirvana and leads out from the house of Saṃsāra.

O Viṣaṅgame! O Paśupati! O Puṣpagarbha!
May there be well-being for me and for all sentient beings, from all fears, calamities, misfortunes, and afflictions; svāhā!

This, O Mahābrahmā, is that Queen of Vidyās named Mahāsāhasrapramardanī, the sūtra that liberates from all seizing spirits; it is the Buddha-seal of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā. Sealed by this seal, the world—including its gods, humans, and asuras—has entered the city of unsurpassed Nirvāṇa.

And for whose sake the perfectly awakened ones, the pratyekabuddhas, and the śrāvakas— who are like the sands of the Ganges— having previously attained awakening, have attended upon the perfectly awakened ones, the pratyekabuddhas, and the śrāvakas as parents, objects of veneration, and those in the position of gurus; and for whose sake they have practiced the holy life and maintained ethical discipline.
Generosity has been practiced, the perfection of compassion has been fulfilled,
the conduct of a bodhisattva has been accomplished, the attainment of enlightenment has been achieved, omniscience has been realized, and Māra has been defeated.
Then Brahmā Sahāpati, Śakra the lord of the gods, and the four Great Kings, with one voice, one mind, and one tone, paid homage to the Blessed One and said:

and they run about in the air at a height of seven palm trees.

may the ascetic Gautama protect us!

May we go to that same destination as those who harbor malice toward the Perfectly Awakened One and those who shed his blood, if we should ever cast away this seal.
His head shall split into seven pieces like the cluster of an arjaka flower;
we shall have our limbs smeared by the yakṣa-disease and become disfigured.
Having mastered this *Sāhasrapramardanī-sūtra* spoken by the Jina,
we shall proceed according to our own will.
And at that time, in the great city of Vaiśālī, all fears, calamities, misfortunes, and afflictions were completely stilled.

And the Licchavis of Vaiśālī were liberated from all diseases and ailments; endowed with every happiness, they came to possess unwavering faith in the Buddha.
They became endowed with verified clarity regarding the Dharma;
they constantly and perpetually delighted in making offerings to the Three Jewels, dwelling in great festivity.
Flocks of birds—swans, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, peacocks, ruddy geese, kunāras, jīvañjīvakas, and others—warbled sweetly.
Free from bodily affliction, like *kiṃnaras* returning from the cycle of rebirth,
unstruck jeweled vessels resounded;
and drums, conchs, clay drums, small drums, lutes, and flutes played spontaneously, even though they remained exactly where they were placed.
Pomegranate, bilva, āmalaka, nyagrodha, aśvattha, plakṣa, kapittha, udumbara, śāla, tāla, tamāla, tilaka, and campaka trees emitted various fragrances;
and thousands of deities let out cries of "Hīhī," and from the sky—
A rain of flowers fell,
and a superhuman fragrance appeared in the world.
Then the four Great Kings, with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Blessed One:
"Venerable Blessed One, this *Mahāsāhasrapramardanī*, the King of Sūtras, is a discourse on the Dharma that is the seal of the Buddha, which liberates one from all seizing spirits (*graha*).

and he shall be invincible against all who would cause him harm.
Therefore, one who wishes to bind the boundaries of a kingdom should bathe well, eat the three white foods, and avoid the five kinds of impure meat.

having strewn flowers upon the ground in the middle of the royal capital, various fragrances should be burned as incense.

and every day, the vidyā should be recited once.
In this way, the kingdom will be liberated.

In this manner, having cleared away all refuse from the villages, royal capitals, sites, monasteries, temples, fields, halls, trees, fruits, greenery, gardens, cow-pens, and livestock sheds; having kindled a fire of *khadira* and jujube wood; having strewn the ground with flowers; having made the gate-halls beautiful and perfumed them with various fragrances; and having smeared all the seeds with clarified butter, they should be scattered in the four directions.

Various colored threads should be cast into the fire and tied across the doorway; those belonging to the animal realm should be led out and then brought back in; and the vidyās should be recited. Having written them down and tied them together, they should be raised up and worshipped.

In front of the sick person, one should place either an image of the Buddha or a relic of the Buddha; having set it upon a high seat or a pedestal, one should also place an image of Brahmā, an image of Śakra, or an image of the Four Great Kings, and having formed the four mudrās, they should be established there.

and may food, drink, and medicine be provided for the ill.

gave him a divine medicine from the scripture that was like nectar.

and may every offering as well become nectar-like medicine.
By the splendor of the Buddha Vipaśyin and the power of Śikhin,

Diseases born of wind, diseases born of bile, diseases born of phlegm, and those born of the combination of all three—may all diseases be destroyed. May there be well-being for me and for all sentient beings at all times from all fears. Svāhā!

The Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and those who are the Śrāvakas of the Buddhas;
Brahmā, Indra, the World-Protectors, and the lords of the Yakṣa generals.

by their heroism and splendor, cut off the activity of the Vetāḍas.
Diamond-jewels are shattered; fire consumes fuel;
clouds are dried up by the wind; and trees are withered by the sun.

by various fragrances and flowers likewise, may all evils be driven away.

One who desires to liberate [others] from goiter, erysipelas, dysentery, insanity, swellings, pustules, fistula-in-ano, and those who have ingested poison, should— having bathed well, being well-adorned, and seated upon an auspicious throne— recite this vidyā with the splendor of all the Buddhas,
the splendor of the Pratyekajinas, and the vigor of the Arhats and of all mantra-holders.

Through Kauṇḍinya’s prior attainment, through Ānanda’s learning,

by the heroism of the generals, and by the prosperity of Hārītī.

Now, therefore, one who desires not to be defeated by strife, quarrels, conflicts, disputes, foreign armies, or enemies should first perform worship at a great shrine (mahācaitya);
and this Queen of Spells (vidyārājñī), the Destroyer of the Great Trichiliocosm (Mahāsāhasrapramardanī), should be set in motion.
By the Buddha, the Māras were conquered and unrighteousness by the Dharma;
by the Saṅgha, the heretics were conquered, and by Indra, the Asuras were conquered;
by the Asuras, Soma was conquered, and by Vainateya, the ocean.
The quarters are conquered by fire, and fire is overcome by water;
the clouds are vanquished by the wind, and the diamond is ground down by the thunderbolt.
By truth the gods abide; by truth the earth is established.
Truth is the Buddha and the Dharma; may truth conquer, not falsehood!

unconquered one, upholder of the Dharma, upholder of the earth!

The adversaries have been conquered and all evils have been defeated;
then the Teacher, the Omniscient One, spoke this verse:
By always grasping the names of Akṣobhyarāja, Avalokiteśvara, Amitābha, Nemi, Ratnārci, Meru, and Vajra, one shall never experience fear or trepidation.
Whoever recites the names of these eight of great splendor for the sake of receiving grace— for that person whose body has been rendered pure, neither fire, nor poison, nor weapon shall prevail.
If, when they have arrived at the place of execution in the presence of a sharp weapon and an executioner,
they call Avalokiteśvara to mind, those weapons shall fall apart into pieces.
Even if a weapon were seized, it would break and fall from their hand to the ground;
nothing at all would strike their body, except for what was caused by past karma previously committed.
All the gods together spoke this verse:
"Homage be to you, O Buddha of infinite range; homage be to you, O Sage who reveals the truth!
By being established in the truth, you liberate all beings; may all our desires become fruitful."
For me and for all sentient beings, svāhā!
Then Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, rose up with palms joined in reverence:
"This well-spoken vidyā is the Destroyer of the Great Thousandfold World."
I shall proclaim this knowledge which brings benefit to children;
I pay homage to the Buddha, the Hero, the King of Dharma, the source of all that is auspicious.
By whom the knowledge was first revealed in Jambudvīpa for the sake of the sublime Dharma and the Saṅgha, the supreme assembly.
Having prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, Brahmā spoke these words:
"The Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and those who are the Śrāvakas of the Buddhas—"
The sages, the world-protectors, and all the deities as well—
all these have arisen from this world of humans.
"O great sage, there are terrible rākṣasas here who guard the womb;
they cannot even be seen by you, nor can they be perceived in the four directions."
For those women whose sons are not born and whose embryos do not remain stable,
the sense faculties become utterly deluded by the union of man and woman.
They destroy the seed of the son, whether it be at the stage of the *kalala* or the *budbuda*; and even when a woman has conceived a fetus in her womb, she gives birth but does not find relief.
I shall declare their names; O Lord of the World, listen to me:
Mañjuka, Mṛgarāja, Skanda, Apasmāra, and Muṣṭika.
Mātṛkā, Jāmikā, Kāminī, and likewise Revatī; Pūtanā, Mātṛnandā, Śakunī, and Kaṇṭhapāṇinī.
Mukhamaṇḍitikā and Ālambā roam across the entire earth;
these fifteen grahas are terrifying to children.
Just as those possessing the characteristics of the breast seize children, so too,
when one is seized by Mañjuka, the eyes roll back.
When seized by the King of Beasts, there is violent vomiting;
when seized by Skanda, the child trembles in his limbs.
One seized by epilepsy emits foam and saliva;
one gripped by a fist-clenching spirit does not release his clenched fist.
One who is possessed by a *mātṛkā* breast-suckles and laughs;
however, one who is possessed by a *jāmikā* does not delight in the breasts.
One seized by Kāminī weeps while fast asleep;
one seized by Revatī gnaws his tongue with his teeth.
One seized by Pūtanā coughs and likewise breaks wind;
one seized by Mātṛnandā, however, will manifest various forms.
For one seized by Śakunī, a foul-smelling stench blows forth;
for one seized at the throat and hands, the throat becomes completely constricted.
If seized by Mukhamaṇḍī, one suffers from fever and purging;
if seized by Ālambā, hiccup and labored breathing arise.
In that regard, I shall describe the form by which they terrify children:
like the king of beasts appearing in the form of a gentle cow, or like a deer.
Skanda appears in the form of a youth; Apasmāra is like a jackal;
Muṣṭikā is in the form of a crow; and Mātṛkā is in the form of a goat.
Jāmikā takes the form of a horse, Kāminī the form of a bellows;
Revatī takes the form of a dog, and Pūtanā the form of a pig.
Mātṛnandā [is subdued] by a cat; Śakunī, who has the form of a bird, [by a cock];
Kaṇṭhapāṇī by a cock; and Mukhamaṇḍikā by an owl.
Taking the form of the collarbones, these frighten children;
they are the terrible stealers of semen, causing terror to boys.
"I shall bring them together, drawn by the noose of the sūtra;
there is a great yakṣa general named Gandharva, known as Candana."
Having given him a letter and a seal, he should dispatch him as a messenger with these words:
"Subdue those fierce ones; you must capture those fifteen planets."
At that very moment, he brought forth those who were oppressed by the fivefold bonds;
then Mahābrahmā, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the Lord of the World.
These very beings destroy the seeds of living creatures;
I shall inflict punishment upon them in the presence of the Lord of the World.
She whose son is not born, or whose son, once born, is seized [by spirits],
should have female disciples practice the True Dharma on the eighth and fourteenth days.
Having fully worshipped the caitya, well-bathed and beautifully adorned,
they covered the ground with mustard seeds and filled it with flowers and perfumes.
One should have one hundred knots made with a five-colored thread;
then, at the time of midnight, standing in a fist-like posture, one should take mustard seeds.
They say it was created by Brahmā and was shaken by Brahmā;
it brings benefit to young boys for as long as twelve years.
Whoever should transgress this thread of knowledge fashioned by Brahmā,
his head shall split into seven pieces like the blossom of an arjaka tree.

*aṅge vaṅge bhaṅge bhavane*.

O Aṅganā! O Alaphā! O Talaphā! O Prakarṣaṇī! Svāhā!
May the fetus be established quickly; may the sense faculties develop properly. May those dwelling in the womb be happy, and may those born not perish.
May the fetus remain healthy and be delivered in due time.
[Offer] threads of various colors, unbroken grains, and white mustard seeds.
"This protection has been fully proclaimed; may the children live for a long time.

May the fetus be protected; may the children rejoice in happiness.
May it be thus: *bodhi bodhi*.

Then the fifteen planets, who always feed upon blood,
having paid homage with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Lord of the World:
Wherever this sutra may be— in a city, a village, or even a house—
there the foolish shall not die, wherever these well-spoken words abide.
O Great Sage, we shall follow according to your rain;
homage to the Blessed Buddha, homage to Brahmā; may [all things] be accomplished!
May the mantra-words deliver this knowledge; may Brahmā consider it, svāhā!
Then the great king Vaiśravaṇa, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder and with palms joined in reverence,
paid homage to the Blessed One and said:
"Venerable Blessed One, whatever disciple should take up, preserve, recite, teach, or master this Mahāsāhasrapramardanī Sūtra, by that person who is well-versed in the scriptures— "
Yoga must be practiced.
One should be devoted to the worship of the caityas.
On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days, having performed a grand worship of the caitya of this yakṣa, the vidyā should be recited.
On the eighth day, four royal messengers attend upon him in the presence of the Great Kings and proclaim his name.
On the fourteenth day, they attend upon him in the presence of the Four Great Kings and proclaim his name.
On the fifteenth day, the Four Great Kings themselves attend upon him and proclaim his name.
"Out of compassion for the welfare of all sentient beings, this disciple of the Blessed One who takes up, maintains, recites, and masters this Mahāsāhasrapramardanī Sūtra—
O Venerable Blessed One, we four Great Kings shall provide for him with zeal the requisites of robes, alms-food, bedding, and medicines for the sick; and he shall be honored."
He will be held in high esteem, honored, and worshiped by all sentient beings, as well as by kings and the great ministers of kings.

He will be worthy of worship among the followers of other sects, the śramaṇas, the brāhmaṇas, and the parivrājakas; even when situated among friends and enemies alike, he will be treated with respect.
Furthermore, that faithful son of good family or daughter of good family must remain pure.
One should possess a pure body and excellent clothing, ornaments, bedding, and requisites;
one must not obtain a poor location, nor associate with evil friends, nor dwell in an unsuitable place.
And before whichever person possessed by a spirit or a planet this sutra named *Mahāsāhasrapramardanī* shall be recited:
The Four Great Kings themselves will provide for his protection, defense, and guardianship.
Venerable Blessed One, such is the great supernatural power of this Mahāsāhasrapramardanī Sūtra that, even in whosever house it shall take up residence for but a single night and day,
non-human beings shall find no opportunity to enter for as long as a year.
And he who shall uphold this *Mahāsāhasrapramardanī-sūtra* will become worthy of homage by the entire host of living beings.
When he so desires, the four Great Kings will manifest themselves for his welfare;
how much more so, then, other yakṣas and rākṣasas?
For what reason? Because those who possess any knowledge whatsoever in the world will provide it for the benefit of sentient beings.
These mantra-words are for them the most excellent, supreme, best, distinguished, and highest;
profound and vast, immeasurable, difficult to penetrate, and uncommon—this is the seal of the Dharma.
Then Indra, the thousand-eyed king of the gods and lord of Śacī,
standing with palms joined in reverence and having paid homage to the Lord of the World, spoke.
This well-spoken knowledge brings benefit to all the world;
I shall proclaim this knowledge together with its mantras and medicinal herbs.
Śirīṣa flower, apāmārga, agaru, kaṭakāphala, śaileya, eḍamañjiṣṭhā, sūkarī, markaṭī, and jayā.
Paripelava, rasā, vīrā, sāmaka, tagara, busā,
candana, āvartana, kuṣṭha, nakha, patrakata, and varā.
Priyaṅgu, rocanā, spṛkkā, mustard seeds, realgar, cinnamon,
saffron, and a coloring agent combined with asafoetida and leaves.
And this wick made from these [substances], when combined, liberates one from all seizing spirits;
it is prescribed as an eye-salve for all transformations caused by malevolent beings.
By holding this, one is liberated from the thunderbolts, lightning, and arrows of the spirits;
it should be smeared upon great trees and likewise upon great shrines.
For he who sees that place has no fear of spirits from it;
there is no standing ground there for spirits, nor for others who wish him harm.
One should also smear drums, conchs, clay drums, and small kettledrums [with the ointment],
so that as long as their sound is heard today, the circles of spirits tremble with fear.
Or one may smear the excrement of village-dwelling birds;
wherever that bird goes, whether to a direction or to the far reaches of the horizon, [the enemy shall follow].
There is no place there for living beings, nor for others who seek one's harm;
one should cast [the substance] into the currents of rivers, into ponds, or wherever else may be.
For a league all around there, well-being and peace shall prevail,
even amidst the falling of weapons and the encounter with enemy armies.
It should be applied to all vital points (*marmas*); one will cross over [these ailments] in safety, as well as in cases of goiters, hemorrhoids, erysipelas, and pustules.
One who has been bitten by a venomous snake or has drunk poison will be quickly liberated after drinking this;
by anointing the body with it, all *kākhorda* spells are cut asunder.
The resolution of disputes is accomplished, and one is released from the king's gate;
the unaccomplished attains accomplishment, and the powerless attains lordship.
One without a son obtains a son; one without wealth obtains wealth;
he shall accomplish all those mantras up to the level of the Vidyādharas.
This [mantra] shall also apply to those born as animals and to the fruits of trees;
for this wise Vidyādhara, it brings about peace and auspiciousness.
In that regard, there are mantra-words which are Indra’s speech, as follows:
*syād yathedam* / *akrame* / *vikrame* /
O you who are the sound of reality!
O you who have entered into reality!
O burner!
Dhadhare / Dharadhare / Dadhini /
Nikhume / Khukhume / Khakha khakha /
O Sāraṅgame!
O Candra!
O Capale!
Halime / Hale, O doe, svāhā!
May there be well-being for me and for all sentient beings from all directions and intermediate directions; svāhā!
All evils are destroyed; svāhā!
Then Brahmā, Śakra, the world-protectors, Maheśvara,
all the yakṣa generals, and Hārītī with her children [approached].
With palms joined in reverence, they spoke with one voice and one tone:
"He possesses the radiance of a thousand suns and the splendor of the full moon."
In the world with its gods and humans, no one equal to you is found;
you are inconceivable, well-employed, and the subduer of yakṣas and rākṣasas.
The vidyā named Rājapramocanī protects dispassion; the great queen named Sāhasrapramardanī brings about auspiciousness.
Victorious in battle and conflict, the crusher of all enemies—
this supreme sūtra is for the sake of protection in this world of great violence.
"Homage to you, O hero among men; homage to you, O supreme among men.
Having paid obeisance with palms joined, they vanished right there.
Then, at the time of evening, the Blessed One rose from his seclusion and addressed the monks:
"Monks, take up the Mahāsāhasrapramardanī-sūtra; preserve it, recite it, and master it.
That shall come to pass."
For the long-term benefit, welfare, happiness, and peaceful dwelling of the world including its gods,

monks, whichever of my disciples should perform a protective binding and a consecration even for a withered tree by means of this *Mahāsāhasrapramardanī-sūtra*, [it shall ensure] its leaves, flowers, and fruits.
How much more so, then, would they arise for a body endowed with consciousness, except through the ripening of previous karma?
Thus addressed, those monks said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Blessed One, regarding these five great protection sūtras that have been spoken—
namely as follows:"
The *Mahāsāhasrapramardanī*,
the *Mahāmāyūrī*, the *Mahāśītavatī*, the *Mahāpratisarā*, and the *Mahāmantrānusāriṇī*—
these should be recited as authorized by the Blessed One, who has renounced the five kinds of impure food.
The going forth has been declared to depend upon alms-food as one's sustenance.

Yet, Blessed One, alms-food free from the five kinds of meat is small; that which is mixed with the five kinds of meat is much more abundant. In this regard, Blessed One, how should we conduct ourselves?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to those monks:
"Therefore, monks, whoever should uphold this Mahāsāhasrapramardanī Sūtra,
by him this indestructible dhāraṇī should be upheld for the sake of self-protection."
Therefore, having taken up the alms-bowl, one should generate the perception of repulsiveness toward food;
regarding alms-food mixed with the five kinds of impurities, one should generate the perception of it being free from those five impurities;
and regarding all conditioned phenomena, the perception of impermanence.
One should cultivate the perception of suffering in the impermanent,
the perception of non-self in what is suffering,
and the perception of impurity in what is non-self.
Whence come the five objects of attachment, or to whom do the five objects of attachment belong? Who is it that consumes the five objects of attachment?
There is no sentient being; whence, then, could there be a sentient being?
That being is not to be apprehended;

and therein, food should be prepared mixed with the five kinds of meat. For self-protection, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days, [an offering should be made] by a girl of royal lineage who has bathed well and is beautifully adorned.

For the sake of physical beauty, one should spend a day and night; having caused a fourfold red thread to be made and taken up by means of the five precepts, the vidyā should be recollected while holding the mantra.
Having tied a knot, that thread should be cut with a new blade and burned. Alternatively, having filled a jewel-vessel with water, covered it with flowers, and fumigated it with various perfumes—
This vidyā should be recited until the produced thread appears in the vessel;
having tied it upon the hand, it should be recited.
Deceived by the Brahmins, the Protector Śākyasiṃha was offered poisoned food by Girigupta.
Then the Teacher, having accepted [the food] and rendered it free of poison for those who eat, said:
"By this word of truth, may the food become nectar."
From the deity Vipaśyin, from Śikhin, from Viśvabhū,
and from the deities Krakucchanda and Prasanna, [the Buddhas] possess great powers.
The lords of gods named Kanaka, as well as those of Śrīmān Kāśyapa,
and the Brahmā-lords, sovereigns of the three realms, were all pleased with the Lion of the Śākyas.
The four world-protectors, Māṇibhadra, Maheśvara,
the rākṣasī Mahākālī, and likewise Caṇḍacaṇḍālinī.
May they accept this flower, this incense, and my offering;
being gratified and honored, may they purify this food.
May they make for me that which is mixed with the five kinds of impure food free from those five;
I shall eat all food that is unmixed with the five kinds of impure food.
May the essences of the earth be the foundation for all groups of seeds;
may they be mixed with all food, or remain unmixed, for me.
Just as a thread that has been cut or burnt becomes so again,
so may they make my food mixed with [impurities] unmixed for me.
It may be as follows:
*khakhame* / *khakha khakha* / *khukhume*.
Sime sime / Sihune / Simi sime /
Svasti, svasti, svasti, svasti! Śānti, śānti, O essence of the supreme! Just as a necklace mixed with the five kinds of impure food becomes free from impurity, [so too is this offering purified].
May they make it true, just as the thread was burnt by that [fire].
It may be as follows:
kalake / kalale / balanikaruṇalāye / khalume /
Svāhā to the one who transfers into the fire!
I go for refuge to the Buddha Vipaśyin;
and to the Buddha Śikhin, the Sugata Viśvabhū;
and to the Buddha Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa.
And to the fearless Śākyamuni Gautama—
having performed the worship of the bodies of these seven supreme among men with flowers, perfumes, body, speech, and mind, I, with a serene heart, go for refuge.
In these Buddhas of great supernatural power, there are deities who have placed their faith;
those deities, joyful and elated, constantly perform acts of peace.
May there be well-being for me and for all sentient beings! Svāhā!

The Blessed One said this, and the monks, those bodhisattvas, and the entire assembly— including the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas— rejoiced and highly praised what the Blessed One had spoken.
The Noble Mahāyāna Sūtra entitled "The Destroyer of the Great Trichiliocosm" is completed.
